target: Yufei Zhao, Probabilistic Methods in Combinatorics (MIT 18.226 lecture notes)

crossing_number.note: Mathlib has no planarity, crossing number, or Euler formula. Not a node in any planned phase.

heilbronn.note: Integral geometry over R^2; the algebraic alternative needs Pick's theorem. Neither is in Mathlib.

high_girth.note: Needs a theory of G(n,p); should be its own phase.

random_greedy.note: Continuous [0,1] construction; needs a discretisation designed first.

distinct_sums.note: Section 4.6 (Erdos distinct subset sums), DONE. Stated finitely and explicitly, no o(1): 3*2^n <= 8*sqrt(n)*M + 4 for any upper bound M on the a_i, i.e. the largest element is at least (3*2^n - 4)/(8 sqrt n). Chebyshev at t = sqrt(n)*M puts three quarters of the 2^n subsets within t of the mean; distinctness makes those sums distinct integers in an interval of length 2t. Non-vacuity checked by instantiating at n = 1 and at a = (1,2) on two elements, both with decide-checked distinctness.

chebyshev.note: Chebyshev over a finite weighted space, with wmean/wvar. Mathlib's is MeasureTheory-only. Wanted by chapters 4, 5, 9.

gnp_weights.note: G(n,p) as finite Bernoulli weights: bweight, sum_bweight, sum_bweight_superset (weight p^#B for a fixed edge set), sum_bweight_disjoint. Take alpha := Sym2 V.

random_triangle.note: First-moment identity C(n,3) p^3, with the second moment and the variance bound now also proved. The n -> infinity threshold statement remains deliberately unstated.

subgraph_threshold.note: Expected number of labelled copies of a fixed H is (#embeddings) * p^e(H). The asymptotic threshold statement stays deferred.

thresholds.note: Needs the weighted-counting layer; state in explicit finite-n form.

clique_number.note: Expected k-clique count is C(n,k) p^C(k,2). First-moment half; the n -> infinity threshold is not stated.

first_moment.note: The first moment method, once: patterns of size m are contained with total weight #patterns * p^m. Instances: 4.1, 4.2, 4.4.

second_moment_method.note: Where a count vanishes the weight is at most wvar/wmean^2. The positive half of every threshold.

second_moment_pair.note: Second moment of a pattern count: sum over pairs of p^#(union). Two patterns are both present iff their union is.

random_triangle_second.note: Triangle-free graphs carry weight at most Var/(C(n,3)p^3)^2. Remaining work in 4.1 is the overlap analysis bounding Var.

chernoff.note: Theorem 5.0.1 via the MGF method. Requires 0 < n, which the notes leave implicit. Real.cosh_le_exp_half_sq is upstream.

chernoff_two_sided.note: Corollary 5.0.3. The lower tail is the upper tail of the complement, so S -> S^c gives equal cardinality and one application of the one-sided bound suffices.

chernoff_bounded.note: Theorem 5.0.5 is Hoeffding's inequality, which Mathlib has in MeasureTheory form (SubGaussian.lean), together with Hoeffding's lemma. Earlier recorded as deferred; that was wrong -- the finite framework cannot state it, but the mathematics is upstream.

chernoff_bernoulli.note: Theorem 5.0.7, DONE. Upper tail for Bernoulli coordinates with DIFFERING probabilities: with mu = sum p i, the weight of the subsets of size at least (1+eps) mu is at most exp(-mu((1+eps) log(1+eps) - eps)). Stated with the exact exponent, not an O() estimate -- t = log(1+eps) is the true minimiser of the MGF bound, so no slack. Checked numerically at seven parameter settings including the degenerate p = 0 case, where both sides equal 1 exactly.

discrepancy.note: Theorem 5.1.1 with the explicit constant 2 rather than O(.). Requires 3 <= #F, which the notes gloss.

restriction.note: Counting subsets of V by a property of S inter A factors as 2^#(V\A) times the count over A.powerset. Lifts a per-edge bound to the whole colouring space.

pweights.note: Independent coordinates with per-element probabilities. sum_pweight and sum_pweight_superset (a fixed B is contained with weight prod over B of p i). Needed by 5.0.7 and by random graphs with varying edge probabilities.

overlap.note: Two vertex sets span exactly the edges of their intersection in common; with card_spannedEdges_union this gives #(E_s union E_t) = C(#s,2) + C(#t,2) - C(#(s inter t),2). The combinatorial heart of every subgraph second moment.

variance_identity.note: wvar = E[X^2] - (E X)^2 when the weights total 1. Turns a computed second moment into a variance.

pair_counting.note: At most C(3,2)*n = 3n triples meet a fixed triple in >= 2 vertices: such a t' is insert v u for a 2-subset u of t. Checked: 10 actual vs bound 18 at n=6, 13 vs 21 at n=7.

variance_triangles.note: Var <= 3 n C(n,3) p^3. Pairs sharing at most one vertex span exactly 6 edges and cancel against E[X]^2 term by term; only overlapping pairs survive.

fkg_upstream.note: Fortuin-Kasteleyn-Ginibre, in Mathlib/Combinatorics/SetFamily/FourFunctions.lean, via Ahlswede-Daykin. Mathlib also has holley, four_functions_theorem and Harris-Kleitman.

harris_fkg.note: Bridge: product measures are log-modular (pweight_mul_pweight, with equality), so Mathlib's fkg applies and gives E[f]E[g] <= E[fg].

fkg_random_graphs.note: Monotone (upward-closed) events correlate under a product measure. With alpha := Sym2 V this is 'monotone graph properties correlate in G(n,p)'.

fkg_triangle.note: Concrete instance: containing a triangle correlates with any monotone property. Needs hasTriangle_mono and a DecidablePred instance for HasTriangle.

azuma.note: Azuma-Hoeffding, in Mathlib SubGaussian.lean. Covers 9.1-9.2 in MeasureTheory form.

talagrand.note: THEOREM 9.5.11 (Talagrand's inequality, general form). STATEMENT COMMITTED, published as a task. In counting form #A * #{x : t <= d_T(x,A)} <= |beta|^(2n) exp(-t^2/4). Unlike the bounded differences inequality, whose bound degrades as exp(-t^2/n), this one has NO n in the exponent -- which is the whole point of the section. The proof is an induction on the number of coordinates using Holder's inequality, plus the delicate elementary fact inf over lambda in [0,1] of exp((1-lambda)^2/4) r^(-lambda) <= 2 - r for r in (0,1]; the notes prove neither. DESIGN NOTE: the sample space is the uniform product Fin n -> beta, as in 9.1, rather than a product of distinct factors with an arbitrary product measure; the notes' applications reach that generality by padding coordinates, the device ChromaticConcentration.lean already uses for graphs.

shearer.note: Theorem 10.4.5 (Shearer's lemma). Proved by splitting at the right place: the entropy side supplies three properties of S -> H(X_S), and everything after that is a statement about set functions. Checked against the classic instance: the three 2-element subsets of a 3-tuple cover each coordinate twice, giving 2 H(X) <= H(X_12) + H(X_02) + H(X_01).

lll.note: Asymmetric LLL, proved. Two inductions: lll_peel (inner, on the index set) and lll_key (outer, strong induction on cardinality). Kept multiplicative throughout -- no division by a probability not known to be positive. Now a corollary of lll_lopsided (the inequality hypothesis), which subsumes it.

lll_symmetric.note: Symmetric LLL at x i = 1/(d+1), needing 1/e <= (d/(d+1))^d from 1 + t <= exp t. Requires 0 < d: at d = 0 the choice x i = 1 violates the asymmetric form's x i < 1, and that case is separately trivial. Textbooks leave this implicit.

block_independence.note: Properties on disjoint coordinate blocks factor, by the bijection S -> (S inter C, S inter (V \ C)). The counting form of the independence hypothesis every LLL application must discharge. Checked numerically: both sides give 9 on Fin 4 with C = {0,1}.

property_b_lll.note: Section 6.2, DONE. A k-uniform hypergraph in which every edge meets at most d others is 2-colourable once e(d+1)2^(1-k) <= 1. Strengthens 1.3's twoColorable_of_card_lt_two_pow: the bound is local, so it applies to arbitrarily large hypergraphs. Non-vacuity checked by instantiating at two 4-edges sharing a vertex on 7 points with d = 1.

independence_bridge.note: P(A inter A') = P(A) P(A') for events determined by disjoint coordinate blocks. The reusable discharge of the LLL independence hypothesis: an application exhibits the blocks and checks disjointness.

monoEvent_determined.note: Monochromaticity on edge i depends only on the colours of edge i's vertices -- the fact that discharges the LLL independence hypothesis for 6.2.

monoEvent_card.note: A k-edge is monochromatic under exactly 2 * 2^(n-k) colourings, i.e. probability 2^(1-k). Proved through DeterminedBy.card_eq: the monochromatic traces on the edge are exactly the empty set and the edge. Checked numerically at (n,k) = (4,2) and (5,3), both giving 8.

unifColoring.note: The uniform weight on the 2^n colourings; probability is counting.

unif_independence.note: Independence for the uniform colouring in the exact shape the local lemma wants: events determined by disjoint blocks of vertices multiply.

determinedBy_noneOf.note: 'None of the edges in T is monochromatic' is determined by any block containing all of them. Finset induction on T through noneOf_insert.

jansonGroup.note: Chapter 8. Reachable with no new probability layer: the ground set is Sym2 V and the measure is pweight.

fkg_anti.note: FKG for decreasing functions, obtained for free from the order dual: pweight's log-supermodularity is an equality, hence symmetric in meet and join, so Mathlib's fkg transports to (Finset a)^op where Monotone means Antitone.

correlate_anti_family.note: Harris for a whole family: finitely many decreasing events are positively correlated. Induction on the index set.

prob_not_superset.note: P(B not contained in S) = 1 - prod of p over B.

janson_lower.note: Theorem 8.1.1, LOWER BOUND. prod (1 - P(A i)) <= P(no A i occurs), with no hypothesis relating the g i to each other -- overlapping bad sets are the interesting case and the bound holds regardless, because the events 'g i is not contained' are decreasing and correlation only helps. A constant-p corollary janson_lower_const is stated for G(n,p) via bweight_eq_pweight.

janson_upper.note: Theorem 8.1.1 UPPER BOUND, DONE. exp(-mu + Delta/2). Kept multiplicative throughout -- no conditional probabilities, hence no case analysis on whether a prefix has positive probability, which is the same decision 6.1 made for the local lemma. Checked numerically at six configurations, several of them tight (0.625 vs 0.687), which confirms both the exponent and the lower-triangular convention.

entropyGroup.note: Chapter 10. Mathlib has Real.negMulLog and binary entropy but no entropy of a random variable, no subadditivity, no chain rule, no Shearer -- this chapter builds that layer.

gibbs.note: Gibbs' inequality. Carries an explicit absolute-continuity hypothesis because under Mathlib's log 0 = 0 convention the usual statement is FALSE: P = (1/2,1/2), Q = (1,0) gives sum = (1/2) log 2 > 0.

wdistDef.note: Distribution of a random variable under a weight.

wentropyDef.note: Shannon entropy in nats. Pinned down numerically before use: constant RV gives 0, fair coin gives log 2.

entropy_le_log_card.note: The uniform distribution maximises entropy: H(X) <= log |beta|. Gibbs against the uniform Q.

entropy_subadditive.note: Subadditivity H(X,Y) <= H(X) + H(Y). Gibbs against the product of the marginals; absolute continuity is free because a marginal is positive wherever the joint is.

entropy_chain_rule.note: H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|X). Termwise this is Mathlib's Real.negMulLog_mul applied to P(X=b,Y=c) = P(X=b) P(Y=c|X=b). The empty fibres need a separate look -- there the conditional distribution is 0/0 = 0 and does not sum to one -- but both sides vanish on them, so the identity holds with no side condition.

wcondDistDef.note: Conditional distribution; 0 on empty fibres, which is the convention that makes the chain rule unconditional.

wcondEntropyDef.note: H(Y|X): the entropy of Y within each fibre of X, averaged over fibres.

cond_reduces_entropy.note: Conditioning reduces entropy: H(Y|X) <= H(Y). Immediate from the chain rule and subadditivity -- the two are the same fact read in opposite directions. This is the monotonicity Shearer's induction runs on.

entropy_relabel.note: Entropy depends only on the distribution, so relabelling values changes nothing. What lets (b x g) x d and b x g x d be used interchangeably -- needed because Lean's (a,b,c) is a,(b,c) and the pair lemmas associate the other way.

entropy_submodular.note: H(X,Y,Z) + H(X) <= H(X,Y) + H(X,Z). Gibbs against Q(x,y,z) = P(x,y)P(x,z)/P(x), whose total mass is 1 where P(x) > 0 and 0 elsewhere, hence <= 1, which is all Gibbs needs. Absolute continuity again free: the joint is dominated by each marginal.

cond_more_reduces.note: H(Y | X, Z) <= H(Y | X): submodularity re-read through the chain rule. The step Shearer's induction takes for each coordinate.

entropy_fibre_congr.note: Entropy depends only on the fibres: if X and Y determine each other pointwise they have equal entropy. Crucially g and h need NOT be mutually inverse on the whole value types, only along the ranges -- which is what makes it apply to a masked tuple versus a pair of masked tuples, whose value types admit no bijection at all.

maskedDef.note: X restricted to S, represented by masking coordinates outside S to none. Keeps every X_S at one type, avoiding dependent-type bookkeeping. Option beta rather than a default value avoids requiring Inhabited and keeps 'erased' distinguishable from every real value.

tupleEntropyDef.note: The set function S -> H(X_S) that Shearer's lemma is about.

masked_pair.note: Two masks jointly carry exactly the information of the mask of their union.

tuple_submodular.note: Diminishing returns: adding coordinate i to a larger set helps no more than adding it to a smaller one. No hypothesis on i needed.

chain_decomp.note: The chain decomposition of a set function along a linear order; telescopes by peeling off the largest element of S. Pure combinatorics, no entropy.

shearer_submodular.note: Shearer's lemma for ANY normalised monotone submodular set function -- the combinatorial half, with no entropy in it. Indexed family so repeated sets are allowed, which is the generality the applications use.

entropy_le_log_image.note: H(Z) <= log #(values actually attained). Sharper than wentropy_le_log_card, which bounds by the size of the whole value type; the counting applications need the attained count, since that is the quantity the combinatorics is about. Gibbs against the uniform distribution on the image.

entropy_uniform_injective.note: An injective random variable under the uniform weight has entropy log |Omega|. The lower half of every entropy counting argument -- what turns H back into a count.

projSetDef.note: The trace of A on the coordinates in S, recorded as masked tuples so all traces live in one type.

shearer_counting.note: Corollary 10.4.7: if every coordinate is covered k times, #A^k <= product of trace sizes. The conversion is entropy_uniform_injective on the whole tuple (H = log #A exactly) and entropy_le_log_image on each mask.

loomis_whitney.note: Theorem 10.4.3: #A^2 <= product of the three axis-plane shadow sizes for A in three coordinates. The notes' Corollary 10.4.4 (volumes of bodies) follows there by approximating with cubes; the n-coordinate Corollary 10.4.6 is card_pow_le_prod_card_projSet at k = n-1. Checked tight, not merely true: the full 2x2x2 cube has 8 points and three 4-point shadows, 8^2 = 64 = 4*4*4.

bweight_pweight_bridge_done.note: bweight p = pweight (fun _ => p). Without this the two halves of the library cannot be combined: FKG, Harris and Janson are stated for pweight, the variance computations for bweight.

bweight_mem.note: The chance a given coordinate survives is p.

bweight_mem_pair.note: The chance two given coordinates both survive is p^#{i,j} -- the whole content of the variance computation is that this exponent is 1 when i = j and 2 otherwise.

linear_mean.note: Mean of a linear form under bweight p: p * sum a. Verified numerically against brute force at three values of p with non-constant a.

linear_var.note: Variance of a linear form under bweight p: p(1-p) * sum a^2. No general independence lemma is invoked; it falls out of sum_bweight_mem_pair. Verified numerically against brute force at three values of p with non-constant a.

interval_count.note: Counting integers in an interval: a family carrying distinct integer values all inside [lo, hi] has at most hi - lo + 1 members. Needs A nonempty, not just lo <= hi -- for empty A the conclusion can fail outright when hi - lo + 1 < 0, and nonemptiness also supplies 0 <= hi, which Nat.floor_le requires.

uniform_weight_counting.note: bweight (1/2) is the uniform weight 2^(-n) on subsets, so probability is counting.

pweight_mgf.note: The moment generating function for differing probabilities: Finset.prod_add with factors p i * e^t and 1 - p i. Nothing here needs the p i to agree, which is exactly why pweight was worth defining.

harris_mixed.note: Harris' inequality in its MIXED form: an upward-closed A and downward-closed B satisfy P(A and B) <= P(A) P(B). From the increasing case applied to A and the complement of B. This is the form Janson's UPPER bound needs -- there the increasing event is 'this bad set appears' and the decreasing one is 'none of the earlier bad sets appears'.

pweightOnDef.note: The weight of one block of coordinates; pweight is the case D = univ.

pweightOn_norm.note: A block's weights total 1, by Finset.prod_add again.

pweightOn_factor.note: The two blocks' weights multiply to the whole weight.

pweight_split.note: The weighted analogue of card_filter_inter_prod: a condition on the trace in C and one on the trace outside C are independent.

pweight_block_indep.note: Events determined by disjoint blocks are independent for pweight -- the non-uniform analogue of card_inter_mul_of_determinedBy. An application only has to exhibit the blocks and check they are disjoint.

badEventDef.note: The event that the bad set g i survives in full.

badEvent_determined.note: g i surviving depends only on the coordinates of g i -- what makes the far-away part of the family genuinely independent rather than merely correlated.

jansonFactorDef.note: The per-step contraction factor 1 - P(A i) + sum over j in U meeting g i of P(A i inter A j).

janson_step.note: The Janson step. Holds for ANY finite T with no ordering hypothesis: split T into the j whose bad set meets g i (mixed Harris, since A i inter A j is increasing and 'none of M occurs' is decreasing) and those disjoint from it (block independence, since they live on the complementary coordinate block).

janson_prod.note: The multiplicative upper bound. Peels the LARGEST index each time so the peeled set is always a prefix -- the same induction as sum_chain_eq in Chapter 10.

delta_halving.note: The lower-triangular double sum is exactly half of Zhao's Delta. The relation 'share an element' is symmetric and P(A i inter A j) is too, so the ordered sum splits into the j<i and i<j halves and (i,j) -> (j,i) matches them term by term.

janson_full.note: Theorem 8.1.1 in the notes' form, both bounds together. The two halves have nothing in common as proofs: the lower bound is Harris (decreasing events are positively correlated, no hypothesis relating the g i needed), the upper peels the family one index at a time.

orderedTrianglesDef.note: Ordered triangles as functions Fin 3 -> V, so they are already in the shape card_pow_le_prod_card_projSet wants. Checked by #eval: 24 on K4, 0 on a 4-cycle.

orderedEdges_card.note: There are exactly 2m ordered edges. Fibring over the first endpoint turns the count into the degree sum, which is Mathlib's handshake lemma. Checked by #eval: 12 on K4 (m=6), 8 on a 4-cycle (m=4).

projSet_pair_bound.note: The trace on two coordinates injects into a set of pairs. Stated for arbitrary indices and an arbitrary target so the caller supplies only the adjacency fact.

triangle_count.note: The triangle-counting bound t^2 <= (2m)^3 for t the number of ORDERED triangles. NOT a numbered result in the notes -- 10.4's own triangle content is Theorem 10.4.9 about triangle-INTERSECTING families, which is different and still open. Included because it shows card_pow_le_prod_card_projSet is usable off the shelf: same Shearer instance as 10.4.3, plus the observation that a two-coordinate trace consists of ordered edges.

spliceOnDef.note: Take the coordinates in C from f and the rest from g. The whole content of product-space independence.

splice_involution.note: Splicing is an INVOLUTION on pairs: (f,g) -> (splice f g, splice g f) applied twice is the identity. This single observation gives block independence with no case analysis and no subtypes.

determinedOnDef.note: An event on a product space depends only on the coordinates in C.

product_block_indep.note: Events determined by disjoint blocks of coordinates are independent, counting form, on a PRODUCT sample space. Checked numerically on (Fin 2 -> Fin 3): 1 * 9 = 3 * 3.

product_indep_prob.note: The same in probability form, ready for the local lemma's hindep hypothesis.

shearer_triple.note: Theorem 10.4.1, the special case of Shearer: 2H(X,Y,Z) <= H(X,Y)+H(X,Z)+H(Y,Z). Two lines from submodularity plus subadditivity against the pair (Y,Z), which cancels H(X). NOT an instance of PMC.shearer -- that requires all coordinates to share a type, whereas here X, Y, Z may have three different ones.

bregman.note: THEOREM 10.2.1 (Bregman-Minc), DONE: a 0-1 matrix whose i-th row has d_i ones has permanent at most prod_i (d_i!)^(1/d_i). Exponentiating the log form. Checked against the notes' EQUALITY cases, which is the strongest available evidence the constant is right: the all-ones 3x3 matrix has per = 6 = prod (3!)^(1/3), a permutation matrix has per = 1 = prod (1!)^1, and the 2+1 block-diagonal matrix has per = 2 = (2!)^(1/2) (2!)^(1/2) 1. A strict case was checked too (rows {0,1},{0} on Fin 2: per = 1 < sqrt 2).

triangle_intersecting.note: Theorem 10.4.9, DONE. Every triangle-intersecting family of graphs on n labelled vertices has size < 2^(C(n,2)-2). Uses ceil(n/2) rather than floor(n/2) for the split, because card_blocks_containing needs blocks of size >= 2 and ceil(n/2) >= 2 already at n = 3 whereas floor(3/2) = 1; the two choices give the same block size r. Non-vacuity checked with a NONEMPTY family: on 3 vertices {all edges} is triangle-intersecting and 1 < 2^(3-2) = 2.

traceOnDef.note: The trace of a family on A, recorded in Finset of the coercion of A rather than Finset alpha. That is the whole reason the intersecting bound comes out relative to #A instead of the size of the whole ground set, which would be useless.

trace_intersecting.note: If every two members of a family meet INSIDE A, the trace on A has at most 2^(#A - 1) members. Mathlib's Set.Intersecting.card_le does the work; the content is that 'meet inside A' is exactly what makes the traces pairwise non-disjoint.

pigeonhole_two_sides.note: Any set with more than two elements has two distinct members on the same side of a two-part split -- the notes' observation that every triangle has an edge in A_S.

indicDef.note: Indicator encoding of a subset as a Boolean tuple -- the bridge from the tuple form of Shearer's counting corollary to the set-family form the applications use.

cor_10_4_7_sets.note: Corollary 10.4.7 in the notes' own form, for a family of SUBSETS rather than of functions: #F^k <= product of trace sizes. The bridge is that a mask supported on S records exactly the trace on S. Checked tight on the star family: #F = 4 on Fin 3 with traces 2 and 2 on {0,1} and {0,2}, k = 1, so 4 <= 4.

container_style_bound.note: If every trace is intersecting, each factor of Corollary 10.4.7 is at most half of that block's powerset. This is the WHOLE non-arithmetic content of Theorem 10.4.9. Checked tight on the star family: 4 <= 2^3/2 = 4.

trace_card_bridge.note: The two ways of writing a trace -- inside A, or intersected with A -- have equal cardinality.

trace_intersecting_inter.note: The intersecting bound with the trace written as G inter A, which is the form the counting corollary produces.

shearer_order_free.note: DONE. shearer_of_submodular and the whole chain below it (shearer, card_pow_le_prod_card_projSet, card_pow_le_prod_card_image_inter, card_pow_le_prod_of_traces_intersecting, card_projSet_pair_le) no longer require [LinearOrder iota]. The order is needed only by sum_chain_eq's peeling and never appears in a conclusion. The fix that works: Trunc.induction_on over Fintype.truncEquivFin to get an order, then SUBST the named instance binder against Subsingleton.elim -- 'have hDE : inst = LinearOrder.toDecidableEq; subst hDE' -- which makes the whole goal instance-uniform in one step. Converting the hypotheses individually with convert does NOT work. Verified by applying the container bound to {e : Sym2 (Fin n) // not e.IsDiag}, which has no linear order and is the edge type Theorem 10.4.9 needs.

cor_10_4_6.note: Corollary 10.4.6, the n-dimensional Loomis-Whitney inequality: #A^(n-1) <= product of the n complement-of-a-coordinate trace sizes. The n complements-of-a-singleton cover each coordinate exactly n-1 times. Stating it in general REQUIRED the LinearOrder hypothesis to come off the chain first, since an arbitrary index type has no order to supply.

choose_two_identity.note: 2*C(m,2) = m(m-1), division-free so Nat subtraction stays harmless. Depends only on propext.

balanced_split_bound.note: 2(C(a,2)+C(b,2)) <= C(a+b,2) when a and b differ by at most one -- unwound, (a-b)^2 <= a+b. The balance hypothesis is load-bearing, not decorative: checked that a = 7, b = 0 gives 42 > 21. This is the step that turns Theorem 10.4.9's C(n,2) - C(n,2)/r into C(n,2) - 2.

edgeTypeDef.note: The edges of K_V as {e : Sym2 V // not e.IsDiag}. An abbrev, not a def, so the subtype structure stays visible to instance resolution. Chosen because Sym2.card_subtype_not_diag gives #(Edge V) = C(#V,2) free, and because with the LinearOrder hypothesis gone it works directly with the container bound.

edge_pair.note: Every edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Sym2.ind needs the non-diagonality proof reverted first, since it mentions the element being destructed.

edge_map.note: An injection on vertices carries edges to edges.

withinDef.note: The edges with both endpoints in S.

card_within.note: Step (2) of Theorem 10.4.9: the number of edges inside S is C(#S,2). Bijection with Edge of the coercion of S, quoting the same Mathlib count on the subtype. The trick: SURJECTIVITY needs to lift an edge of V with both ends in S to an edge of S, awkward as a function -- but surjectivity is a Prop, so Sym2.ind destructs the edge into an actual pair. Using Finset.card_bij (surjectivity) rather than card_bij' (an explicit inverse) is what makes that available. Checked by #eval: 3, 6, 0 on Fin 4 for {0,1,2}, univ, {0}; and the 10.4.9 block on Fin 5 with |S|=2 gives 1+3=4.

blockDef.note: The block A_S of Theorem 10.4.9: edges inside S together with those inside its complement.

covering_multiplicity.note: Step (3) of Theorem 10.4.9: for a fixed edge, the number of m-element vertex sets putting both endpoints on the same side is C(n-2,m-2) + C(n-2,m). It visibly does not depend on WHICH edge, so the notes' appeal to 'symmetry and averaging' -- which in Lean would mean a transitive action of S_n on edges -- is unnecessary. 2 <= m is required and not cosmetic: at m = 0 the truncated m-2 makes the first term C(n-2,0) = 1 while no 0-set contains both endpoints. Checked at two different edges: Fin 5 with m=2 gives 4 = 1+3, Fin 6 with m=3 gives 8 = 4+4.

card_block.note: The block splits as a disjoint union -- edges inside S and edges inside its complement -- so #(block S) = C(#S,2) + C(n-#S,2). Disjointness holds because an edge has a vertex, which cannot be both in S and outside it.

sum_card_block.note: Counting the pairs (S, e) with e inside a part of S, both ways round.

double_count.note: Step (4) of Theorem 10.4.9, the double-count identity: C(n,m)*r = C(n,2)*k with r the block size and k the number of blocks containing a given edge. Both r and k are CONSTANT, which is why each side collapses to a product. Checked numerically at (n,m) = (6,3) giving 120 = 120 and (7,3) giving 315 = 315.

balanced_split_strict.note: The STRICT form of the balanced-split bound, which is what makes Theorem 10.4.9's conclusion strict. (a-b)^2 <= 1, so once a+b >= 2 there is room to spare; equality in the non-strict version happens only at a+b <= 1.

hasTriDef.note: G contains a triangle. Phrased through a 3-element VERTEX SET rather than three explicit edges, so that no non-diagonality proofs appear in the statement.

block_meets_triangle.note: Every block meets every triangle: two of the triangle's three vertices lie on the same side of S, and the edge between them is in the block.

binomial_tail.note: Section 10.1's binomial tail bound in EXPLICIT form: (sum over i <= k of C(n,i)) * x^k <= (1+x)^n for every x in [0,1]. The notes give this and then take the infimum over x to get 2^(H(k/n)n); the explicit-x form is the one this project wants -- finite, sharp, no o(1) -- and the entropy form follows from it by substituting the minimising x, which is a real-analysis optimisation rather than a combinatorial step. Stated multiplicatively so x = 0 needs no special case. The whole content is that x^k <= x^i for i <= k when x <= 1.

binomial_tail_entropy.note: Section 10.1's entropy bound on the binomial tail, stated ALGEBRAICALLY: sum over i <= k of C(n,i) <= (n/k)^k * (n/(n-k))^(n-k), for 0 < k and 2k <= n. The right side IS 2^(H(k/n) n) -- confirmed numerically to 6 figures at (n,k) = (10,3), (20,4) and (100,10) -- so this is the notes' bound without logarithms, which is sharper in form and needs no Real.log. The 2k <= n hypothesis is not cosmetic and the notes state it too: the minimising x = k/(n-k) exceeds 1 once 2k > n, and sum_choose_mul_pow_le needs x <= 1.

sidorenko.note: Section 10.3, Sidorenko's inequality. Homomorphism densities; Remark 10.3.8 notes the Mobius graph K_{5,5} minus C_10 is the smallest open case, so the section is partly about an open problem.

determinedOn_noneOf.note: The product analogue of determinedBy_noneOf: 'none of the events in T occurs' depends only on a block containing all of their blocks.

product_lll.note: The local lemma packaged for a PRODUCT sample space -- the twin of 6.2's exists_two_coloring_of_local_lemma, and the engine all of 6.3, 6.4 and 6.5 need. Supply the events, the coordinate block each depends on, a bound p on their probabilities and a bound d on how many other blocks each meets; independence is discharged internally from wprob_unifProd_mul_of_determinedOn, so an application never mentions wprob. Usability verified end to end by instantiating it: one event on a 2-coordinate product over 6 values, all seven hypotheses discharged.

trim_enumerate.note: Section 6.3's bridge from 'graph with parts' to a UNIFORM product space: pairwise disjoint parts of size at least k admit an array w : Fin r -> Fin k -> V listing k distinct vertices from each part, with vertices of different parts distinct. This is the notes' 'we may assume |V_i| = k, or else remove some vertices' step, and it is what makes the sample space uniform -- without it the parts have different sizes and the weight would be a product of 1/|V_i|. A transversal built from w is automatically one of the original parts, so trimming loses nothing. Verified on parts of DIFFERENT sizes (4 and 2, enumerated at 2), which is the case trimming exists for.

independent_transversal.note: Theorem 6.3.1, DONE -- by a CONTRIBUTOR, through the Choir loop: task #41 published the statement, it was claimed 36 seconds later, and PR #43 landed a verified self-contained proof that passed all nine checks. The orchestrator proved it concurrently and closed the issue four minutes before the PR arrived, which was a process error: a published task belongs to whoever claims it. The resolution kept both -- Transversal.lean was restored to the exact published base so the contributor's patch applied byte-for-byte, and the orchestrator's modular pieces moved to TransversalBlocks.lean. Check the lease with 'choir orch tasks' before proving anything yourself.

adj_pairs_count.note: Section 6.3's counting core: the ordered adjacent pairs whose first vertex lies in S number at most #S * Delta. Fibre over the first coordinate; each fibre injects into that vertex's neighbourhood. With S = V_i union V_j of size 2k this is the 2k*Delta of the notes. Checked TIGHT on K4 (2*3 = 6) and at 4 on a 4-cycle.

coord_fibres_equal.note: All fibres of a coordinate have the same size; the bijection between two of them is Function.update, replacing the i-th coordinate.

coord_fibre_mul.note: The #beta fibres partition the product, so each has size card(iota -> beta) / #beta.

coord_prob.note: Fixing one coordinate of a uniform product has probability 1/#beta. Every application of exists_avoiding_of_lll needs this: block independence then multiplies it across the coordinates an event pins down. Checked on (Fin 3 -> Fin 4): 16 of 64 for one coordinate, 4 of 64 for two, i.e. 1/4 and (1/4)^2.

janson_lower_tail.note: Theorem 8.2.2 (Janson inequality III), the lower tail. STATEMENT COMMITTED, published as task #42. Bootstraps 8.1.1's upper bound rather than reproving it. The substantial piece is the enlargement: transport pweight and badEvent across a sum type alpha + iota, where the new coordinates create no new overlaps and the parameters come out mu_Y = q mu, Delta_Y = q^2 Delta.

badCountDef.note: Statement-layer definition for 8.2. jansonDelta uses Zhao's ORDERED-pair convention, so 8.1.1 reads exp(-mu + Delta/2).

jansonMuDef.note: Statement-layer definition for 8.2. jansonDelta uses Zhao's ORDERED-pair convention, so 8.1.1 reads exp(-mu + Delta/2).

jansonDeltaDef.note: Statement-layer definition for 8.2. jansonDelta uses Zhao's ORDERED-pair convention, so 8.1.1 reads exp(-mu + Delta/2).

tEventDefs.note: The bad event for 6.3: both chosen slots are the ones joined by an edge. Invalid indices get the empty event, which is never violated, has probability 0, and is determined on the empty block.

tEvent_determined.note: Each 6.3 bad event depends only on the two part-indices in its block.

tEvent_prob.note: A 6.3 bad event has probability 1/k^2, by block independence over the two distinct coordinates it pins down.

tNbr_degree.note: The 6.3 dependency degree is at most 2k*Delta - 1. tPair injects the neighbourhood, plus the event itself, into the ordered adjacent pairs starting in V_i union V_j. The -1 is the self-exclusion from the errata; without it the notes' displayed inequality is false at Delta = 2. Injectivity is where c.1 < c.2.1 earns its keep.

coord_pred_prob.note: A predicate on one coordinate: probability #(allowed values)/#beta. The single-value case summed over the values the predicate allows, counted in Nat first via card_filter_coord_mul so no division appears until the end.

coords_multiply.note: Independent coordinates multiply: an event constraining each coordinate in C separately has probability the product of the per-coordinate probabilities. This is what an application with events on MORE THAN TWO coordinates needs -- 6.4's bad event constrains a vertex's whole out-neighbourhood. Checked on (Fin 3 -> Fin 4): 36 of 64 functions have both coordinates 0 and 1 nonzero, i.e. (3/4)^2 = 9/16.

directed_cycles.note: Theorem 6.4.3 (Alon-Linial 1989). ALL THREE inputs to the probabilistic half are now proved: dEvent (the bad event), wprob_dEvent_le (its probability ((k-1)/k)^delta, checked exact on the directed 4-cycle), and card_digraph_dependency_le (the degree Delta + delta*Delta, checked tight on the same example). What remains: (a) assemble them through exists_avoiding_of_lll to get the LABELLING theorem -- there is an x : V -> ZMod k with every vertex having an out-neighbour labelled x v + 1 -- which is a complete named result on its own; (b) extract a directed cycle of length divisible by k from the colour-incrementing walk, which needs digraph walk machinery Mathlib has for SimpleGraph but not digraphs; (c) the notes' 'final trick' for 6.4.3's exact constant, since the first-pass degree bound only gives k <= delta/(1 + log(1 + Delta + delta*Delta)).

dblkDef.note: The coordinates 6.4's bad event at v depends on: v and its out-neighbours.

digraph_degree.note: 6.4's dependency degree is at most Delta + delta*Delta, counted the notes' own way: at most Delta stepping backward, delta forward, and delta(Delta-1) forward-then-backward. The -1 matters -- v is itself an in-neighbour of each of its out-neighbours and must be excluded -- and it is what turns Delta + delta + delta(Delta-1) into Delta + delta*Delta. 1 <= Delta is needed only to fold those together; at Delta = 0 the relation is empty. This is the FIRST-PASS bound, which is what the straightforward local lemma needs; the notes then find a smaller valid dependency digraph (their 'final trick') to reach 6.4.3's exact constant, and without it one gets k <= delta/(1 + log(1 + Delta + delta*Delta)). Checked TIGHT on the directed 4-cycle: all degrees 1, bound 1 + 1 = 2, and the actual neighbourhood of a vertex has exactly 2 elements.

dEventDef.note: 6.4's bad event at v: no out-neighbour of v carries the next label.

dEvent_prob.note: 6.4's probability bound P(A_v) <= ((k-1)/k)^delta. The event is NOT of the form 'each coordinate in a block satisfies a fixed predicate', because what the out-neighbours must avoid depends on x v; splitting on the value of x v fixes that, since each piece IS of that form and wprob_unifProd_forall applies. Subadditivity over the k pieces then suffices -- the local lemma only wants an upper bound, so no exact computation is needed. Checked EXACT on the directed 4-cycle with k = 2: 8 of 16 labellings, i.e. 1/2 = ((2-1)/2)^1.

dEvent_determined.note: 6.4's bad event at v depends only on dblk r v = {v} union out(v). Both quantities the event mentions -- x v and the labels of the out-neighbours -- live in that block, so the proof is two applications of the block hypothesis. This is the last input the assembly needed.

digraph_labelling.note: Section 6.4's PROBABILISTIC half, complete as a named result: if every vertex of a loopless digraph has out-degree exactly delta and in-degree at most D, and e ((k-1)/k)^delta (D + delta*D + 1) <= 1, then the vertices can be labelled by ZMod k so that EVERY vertex has an out-neighbour carrying the next label. Assembled from exists_avoiding_of_lll with the block dblk r v; the local lemma's hfar is discharged from the definition of the dependency neighbourhood, so the whole degree count enters through card_digraph_dependency_le. This is what 6.4.3's cycle argument consumes; the remaining half of 6.4 is combinatorial, not probabilistic -- extracting a cycle whose length is divisible by k from such a labelling needs digraph walk machinery Mathlib lacks. Non-vacuity checked on the complete digraph on 9 vertices at k = 2: out-degree and in-degree 8, e (1/2)^8 (8 + 64 + 1) = 0.775 <= 1, all six hypotheses discharged.

cycle_extraction.note: Section 6.4's COMBINATORIAL half, and the reason it needs no digraph machinery. Mathlib has walks for SimpleGraph but not for digraphs; instead, choosing at each vertex one out-neighbour carrying the next label packages the labelling as a successor FUNCTION f : V -> V, and a directed cycle is then exactly a periodic orbit of f. Iterating from any vertex repeats in a finite type (Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite), which gives a periodic point; the cycle is its orbit, whose vertices are distinct by Function.iterate_injOn_Iio_minimalPeriod, and since the label increases by 1 per step, returning after p steps forces x u = x u + p, i.e. (p : ZMod k) = 0. A cycle is recorded as c : Nat -> V with r (c n) (c (n+1)), c (n+p) = c n, and injective on Set.Iio p -- no Walk analogue needed. Using the MINIMAL period is what makes the vertices distinct: the raw pigeonhole period need not be a cycle.

cycle_6_4_3_exact.note: Theorem 6.4.3 for out-degree exactly delta: the two halves joined. The choose step is where 'every vertex has AN out-neighbour with the next label' becomes 'THE chosen out-neighbour', which is what makes the orbit argument available. Non-vacuity checked on the complete digraph on 9 vertices at k = 2 (both degrees 8, e (1/2)^8 (8+64+1) = 0.775 <= 1).

cycle_6_4_3.note: Theorem 6.4.3 with the notes' hypothesis, MINIMUM out-degree delta. Obtained from the exact case by DELETING out-edges: choose delta out-neighbours at each vertex (Finset.exists_subset_card_eq) and run the argument on the sub-digraph, whose out-degree is exactly delta and whose in-degree only dropped; a cycle of the sub-digraph is a cycle of the original. The reduction is necessary rather than cosmetic -- the probability bound wants out-degree LARGE while the dependency-degree bound wants it SMALL, so no single inequality on delta serves both, and this is the step the notes leave implicit.

cycle_6_4_3_log.note: Theorem 6.4.3 in the notes' shape: k (1 + log (1 + D + delta*D)) <= delta, i.e. k <= delta / (1 + log (1 + D + delta*D)). The analytic step is (k-1)/k = 1 - 1/k <= exp(-1/k), hence ((k-1)/k)^delta <= exp(-delta/k), so the left side is at most exp(1 - delta/k) M, which is <= 1 exactly when 1 + log M <= delta/k. The notes' constant has delta*D where this has D + delta*D; the gap is the first-pass dependency digraph, and closing it needs their final trick, which only shrinks N and so plugs into the same assembly. Non-vacuity checked on the complete digraph on 25 vertices at k = 2, where 2 (1 + log 601) = 14.8 <= 24.

lll_lopsided.note: Section 6.5's lopsided local lemma (Erdos-Spencer), asymmetric form: the dependency hypothesis is NEGATIVE CORRELATION, P(A_i and none of T) <= P(A_i) P(none of T), an inequality rather than the independence equality. The existing proof already sufficed -- it uses the hypothesis exactly once in a calc chain that only travels upward, so one '=' became one '<=' in lll_key. The independence forms are now one-line corollaries, leaving every 6.2-6.4 application untouched. General lesson: a proof written multiplicatively, with no division, generalizes from equality to inequality hypotheses for free.

lll_symmetric_lopsided.note: The symmetric lopsided form, which is what an application uses: probability at most p, negative correlation outside the neighbourhood, degree at most d, e p (d+1) <= 1. What remains of 6.5 is the Latin-transversal application, where the sample space is a set of permutations and the negative-correlation hypothesis has to be established for random permutations.

unifPerm.note: The uniform weight on Equiv.Perm alpha. Section 6.5's applications live on a sample space of PERMUTATIONS, where unifProd does not reach: the coordinates sigma i are not independent, they are distinct.

perm_swap_count.note: The one device the whole permutation layer rests on: composing with a transposition, sigma -> swap t t' * sigma, is a bijection between the permutations sending i to t and those sending i to t'. Gives the exact probability P(sigma i = t) = 1/|alpha| by fibering over the image of i.

perm_apply_prob.note: P(sigma i = t) = 1/|alpha|, EXACTLY -- the lopsided local lemma's hypothesis is P(A_i and none of T) <= P(A_i) P(none of T) with P(A_i) itself on the right, so an upper bound on P(A_i) would not do.

perm_negative_correlation.note: Fixed-point events are negatively correlated with derangement events: P(sigma i = i and no fixed point in S) <= P(sigma i = i) P(no fixed point in S) whenever i is not in S. The counting core is card_filter_fix_le, the same transposition composed on the left: it cannot create a fixed point at j in S, because that would need sigma j = swap i t j, forcing j = t and sigma t = i, which injectivity rules out since sigma i = i already. This is Theorem 6.5.5's random-injection argument for single-edge matchings. Checked STRICT on Fin 3 with S = {1}: 3 * 1 = 3 < 4, i.e. P = 1/6 < 2/9, so the events are genuinely not independent and the ordinary local lemma does not apply.

derangement_bound.note: Corollary 6.5.6: a uniform random permutation of an n-element type has no fixed point with probability at least (1 - 1/n)^n. The lopsided local lemma with an EMPTY dependency neighbourhood, x_i = 1/n. ERRATUM: the notes write 'Since P(A_i) = 1 - 1/n, we can set x_i = 1 - 1/n'; both are the same slip, since P(A_i) = 1/n and the choice is x_i = 1/n, which is what makes the displayed product (1 - 1/n)^n come out. Checked on Fin 3: 2 of 6 permutations are derangements, so P = 1/3 >= 8/27. The n <= 1 cases are separate -- at n = 1 the bound is 0 and at n = 0 both sides are 1.

perm_extend.note: The one missing ingredient for Theorem 6.5.5 in full generality: a partial injection extends to a permutation that FIXES EVERY POINT OUTSIDE its domain and image. Mathlib's Equiv.extendSubtype does 'something arbitrary outside', and although its construction happens to be the identity off the union, that is not exposed as a lemma -- so this needs either an unfolding of extendSubtype/toCompl through setDiffEquiv or a direct construction. The 'fixes outside' clause is not decoration: 6.5.5's argument needs the column permutation carrying one matching to another to leave every other column alone, or it could create a forbidden pattern elsewhere. STATEMENT COMMITTED, published as a task.

perm_negative_dependence_general.note: Theorem 6.5.5 for arbitrary matchings, the general negative-dependency statement of the random injection model, and then Theorem 6.5.11 (Erdos-Spencer: every n x n array whose every entry appears at most n/(4e) times has a Latin transversal). The single-edge case is proved (perm_negative_correlation); the general case replaces the transposition by the permutation of perm_extend. Reading the notes' proof closely, the case analysis that makes it work is: for an edge (x,y) of a far-away matching, either y lies outside both column sets, and then the permutation fixes y so the edge was already in the original matching, or y is a column of T, and then the preimage lies in the original matching's columns, forcing x into its row set -- contradicting row-disjointness. The notes' displayed hypothesis mentions only disjointness from F_0, which is indeed all that is used.

pair_prob.note: Theorem 6.5.11's probability input: P(sigma i1 = j1 and sigma i2 = j2) = 1/(n(n-1)) for distinct rows and distinct columns. One transposition still suffices -- with the first column held fixed, Equiv.swap moves the second anywhere else and fixes j1 precisely because both columns differ from it. The n-1 rather than n is the constraint sigma i2 != sigma i1: the second cell cannot reuse the first column, which is why the fibering runs over univ.erase j1. Checked on Fin 4: 2 of 24 permutations send 0 to 1 and 2 to 3, i.e. 1/12 = 1/(4*3).

tauRank.note: The number of members of S that a random order tau reveals at or after i -- the count of choices still 'greedily available'. Section 10.2's proof of Bregman-Minc is organised around it.

rank_bijection.note: For each order, EXACTLY ONE member of S has each rank in {1..#S}: the rank is a bijection from S onto that interval, by strict monotonicity (a later element has strictly fewer choices left). Half of the uniformity argument.

rank_symmetry.note: The other half: the ranks are equidistributed across the members of S, because right-multiplying tau by Equiv.swap i i' exchanges the roles of i and i' and preserves S.

rank_uniform.note: THE NOTES' '(Why?)' STEP, proved: under a uniformly random order the rank of a member of S is uniform on {1..#S}. Summing 'exactly one element has rank k' over the members of S and using the swap symmetry gives #S classes of equal size, hence probability 1/#S each. Worth recording that this needs NO order machinery: the obvious route -- pick the k-th smallest element of tau(S) and swap it into place -- needs Finset.orderIsoOfFin and sorted lists, while double counting needs only a transposition. Checked on Fin 3 (uniform over 3 ranks, 2 orders each) and on the proper subset {0,2} (2 ranks, 3 orders each).

rank_expectation.note: Bregman-Minc's per-row bound: E[log(rank)] = log(d!)/d, by averaging log k over k = 1..d. The general form wmean_comp_tauRank takes an arbitrary f, since the distribution -- not the function -- is the content.

dist_entropy_le_log_card.note: A probability vector supported in a finite set T has entropy at most log #T. Stated for a bare DISTRIBUTION rather than a random variable, which is what makes it reusable for conditional distributions -- there the 'random variable' is wcondDist and there is no underlying map to speak of. Generalises 10.1's wentropy_le_log_card_image.

cond_entropy_le_expected_log.note: Conditional entropy is at most the EXPECTED LOG of the conditional support: if Y is always in T(X), then H(Y|X) <= sum_b P(X=b) log #(T b). This is the step of Bregman-Minc that turns entropy back into counting -- in the application T b is the set of columns still free for a row once the earlier rows are known. Fibres of probability zero contribute nothing to either side, so no side condition is needed.

tuple_entropy_insert.note: Extending a mask by one coordinate adds exactly that coordinate's conditional entropy. The pair (masked P, X i) and the mask of insert i P have value types with no bijection between them, so this goes through wentropy_congr, which only asks the two maps to invert each other along the ranges -- the same reason wentropy_masked_pair needed it.

order_chain_rule.note: The chain rule ALONG AN ARBITRARY ORDER: for every permutation tau of the coordinates, H(X_univ) = sum_i H(X_i | X_{predecessors of i under tau}). A telescoping sum over the prefixes of tau (Finset.sum_range_sub), reindexed by tau.symm. This is the structural half of Radhakrishnan's proof of Bregman-Minc: the identity holds for EVERY order, and the argument then averages the resulting bounds over a uniformly random one.

matchSet.note: The permutations selecting a one from every row: the perfect matchings the permanent counts. Verified against the permanent on concrete matrices by decide.

hitSet.note: The rows whose selected column is one of row i's ones. Under sigma this set corresponds bijectively to row i's support, so it has d_i elements (card_hitSet).

avail_eq_rank.note: THE COMBINATORIAL IDENTITY the notes leave implicit: the columns of row i not yet taken correspond, via sigma inverse, to the members of hitSet that tau reveals at or after i. Each one of row i sits in a column sigma j for exactly one row j, and the one is still available precisely when that j has not been revealed. This is what makes the abstract uniformity of tauRank applicable to the matrix.

match_entropy.note: H(sigma) = log(per A): a uniform matching is determined by its coordinates, so wentropy_uniform_of_injective turns the entropy back into a count. The empty case (no matchings) is handled separately, where both sides are 0 under Mathlib's log 0 = 0.

bregman_per_order.note: The bound for ONE FIXED order: log(per A) <= sum_i E_sigma[log N_i(sigma,tau)]. Chain rule along tau, then each conditional entropy bounded by the log of the columns still free. Holds for every tau, which is what makes the averaging step available.

bregman_log.note: The log form of Bregman-Minc: log(per A) <= sum_i log(d_i!)/d_i. The two expectations are exchanged by Finset.sum_comm -- the bound holds for each order, and for each matching the rank is uniform as the order varies. THE KEY POINT of the whole proof: bounding each conditional entropy by log d_i (the naive worst case) would be too lossy; revealing in a random order replaces log d_i by the average of log 1, ..., log d_i.

perm_transpose.note: The permanent is transpose-invariant, by sigma -> sigma inverse. Needed to apply Bregman to the OTHER side of a bipartite graph. Checked on an asymmetric example (rows {0,1},{0} on Fin 2, columns of sizes 2 and 1, permanent 1 both ways).

kahn_lovasz_bipartite.note: Corollary 10.2.2 (Kahn-Lovasz) FOR BIPARTITE GRAPHS: pm(G)^2 <= prod over X of (d_x!)^(1/d_x) times prod over Y of (d_y!)^(1/d_y), i.e. pm(G) <= prod over all 2n vertices of (d_v!)^(1/(2 d_v)). Bregman applied to each side in turn. The NON-bipartite case is not this: it needs pm(G + G) <= pm(G x K_2), which the notes leave as an exercise and which is the actual content of Kahn-Lovasz -- so only the bipartite case is claimed here.

ham_cycles_bregman.note: Theorem 10.2.6's Bregman step: the number of Hamilton cycles of a tournament is at most prod_i (d_i!)^(1/d_i) with d_i the out-degree. The first inequality of the notes' displayed chain -- that a Hamilton cycle IS a 1-factor -- is literally a subset relation in this encoding, so the whole content is Bregman. Getting from here to O(sqrt(n) n!/2^n) needs log-concavity of x -> (x!)^(1/x), a smoothing argument over degree sequences of total C(n,2), and Stirling; the notes omit the first ('One can check (omitted)') and it is a genuine analysis project, so 10.2.6 and 10.2.4 are NOT claimed. Checked on the cyclic tournament on Fin 3 (per = 1, bound 1, equality) and the transitive one (per = 0, since the sink has out-degree 0).

factorial_log_concave.note: Log-concavity of x -> (x!)^(1/x), the step Theorem 10.2.6 omits ('One can check (omitted)'). ERRATUM: the notes display it as g(n)g(n+2) >= g(n+1)^2, which is log-CONVEXITY and is false for every n >= 1 -- at n = 1 it reads 1 * 6^(1/3) >= 2, i.e. 1.817 >= 2. Checked numerically for n up to 4000: the notes' direction fails at every n >= 1 and the concave direction holds at every n >= 1, failing only at n = 0, where (0!)^(1/0) is a convention artifact. So the statement committed has the flipped inequality and the hypothesis 1 <= m. STATEMENT COMMITTED, published as a task.

dirEdges.note: The ordered pairs of adjacent vertices -- the directed edges, of which there are 2m. Checked on K3 (6).

walk3.note: The homomorphisms from the three-edge path: walks x-y-z-w with repetitions allowed. Checked on K3 (24 = 3*2*2*2).

card_walk3.note: hom(P4,G) = sum over directed edges (y,z) of d(y)d(z): a walk is a middle edge together with a neighbour of each endpoint. Fibred over the middle pair.

jensen_log.note: Jensen for log -- the mean of the logs is at most the log of the mean -- derived from GIBBS' INEQUALITY against the uniform distribution on S. Worth having as a named tool: it is AM-GM in the form averaging arguments want.

degree_gibbs.note: sum_v d(v) log d(v) >= 2m log(2m/n), by Gibbs against the uniform distribution on vertices with P(v) = d(v)/2m. This is the notes' H(X) <= log n step, in counting form.

blakey_roy.note: THEOREM 10.3.3 (Blakey-Roy 1965), DONE: Sidorenko's conjecture for the three-edge path, hom(P4,G) n^2 >= (2m)^3. The notes' entropy proof is carried out with NO conditional-entropy machinery: writing the walk distribution's entropy out explicitly, the argument is exactly two applications of Gibbs' inequality -- AM-GM over the middle edge, then the degree sum against the uniform distribution on vertices. That is worth recording: Gibbs' inequality IS the entropy inequality, so a proof using only Gibbs is the entropy proof written out. Checked on K3, where the bound is ATTAINED: 6^3 = 216 = 24 * 9. Equality for regular graphs is the right behaviour, since the random graph is the conjectured minimiser.

blakey_roy_density.note: The same in the notes' density form t(P4,G) >= t(K2,G)^3, which is how Sidorenko's conjecture is stated.

walk4.note: The homomorphisms from C4 = K_{2,2}: closed walks a-b-c-d-a. Checked on K3: 18 = tr(A^4) = 2^4 + 1 + 1.

codeg.note: The number of common neighbours of two vertices. Checked on K3 (1 for distinct vertices, 2 for a vertex with itself).

sidorenko_C4.note: THEOREM 10.3.6's demonstrated case F = K_{2,2}, DONE: hom(C4,G) n^4 >= (2m)^4, i.e. t(C4,G) >= t(K2,G)^4. Grouping a C4-homomorphism by its pair of OPPOSITE vertices gives hom(C4,G) = sum over pairs of codeg^2, and the codegrees sum to sum_v d(v)^2, so two applications of sq_sum_le_card_mul_sum_sq (Cauchy-Schwarz) -- over the n^2 pairs and then over the n vertices -- give the bound. DELIBERATE DEVIATION from the notes: their entropy proof for C4 needs a conditional-independence step this library does not have, while Cauchy-Schwarz needs nothing new. The statement is theirs.

triangleFreeGraphs.note: The triangle-free graphs on n labelled vertices, the objects Question 11.0.1 counts.

graphOfPairs.note: The graph whose edges are a given set of pairs. Used to inject sets of CROSSING pairs into triangle-free graphs.

bipartite_cliqueFree.note: A graph whose every edge crosses a bipartition is triangle-free: two of any three vertices lie on the same side, and same-side vertices are never adjacent.

ekr_lower_bipartition.note: The lower bound of Theorem 11.0.2 for an ARBITRARY bipartition: a split into A and its complement gives 2^(#A * (n - #A)) triangle-free graphs. Stating it for an arbitrary A avoids computing the card of a filter on Fin n and makes the balanced case a one-line corollary. The injectivity needs care: graphOfPairs symmetrises, so Adj u v could come from (u,v) or (v,u), and only one of the two can lie in A x Acomplement -- that is what makes the pair set recoverable from the graph.

ekr_lower.note: THE LOWER BOUND OF THEOREM 11.0.2 (Erdos-Kleitman-Rothschild), DONE: at least 2^(floor(n^2/4)) triangle-free graphs on n labelled vertices, since floor(n/2) * ceil(n/2) = floor(n^2/4). EXACT for every n, with no error term -- the o(n^2) of 11.0.2 lives entirely in the upper bound, which is why this half needs no restatement decision. The upper bound is the container method's whole purpose and needs Theorem 11.1.1 and behind it the hypergraph container theorem. Checked: with A = {0,1} in Fin 4 there are 4 crossing pairs and 16 subsets, so at least 16 of the 41 triangle-free graphs on 4 vertices are produced.

starHom.note: The homomorphisms from the star K_{1,t}: a centre together with t independently chosen neighbours of it. Checked on K3: 12 for t=2 and 24 for t=3.

sidorenko_star.note: Sidorenko's conjecture for STARS, a case of Theorem 10.3.5: hom(K_{1,t},G) n^(t-1) >= (2m)^t. Once hom(K_{1,t},G) is recognised as sum_v d(v)^t -- a centre plus t independent neighbours -- this is exactly the power-mean inequality (pow_sum_div_card_le_sum_pow). Worth recording next to the harder cases because it locates the difficulty in Sidorenko's conjecture: not in trees with a single branch vertex, but in the ones whose entropy bookkeeping needs a genuine chain rule. Checked on K3 at t = 2: (2m)^2 = 36 = 12 * 3, equality, as it must be for a regular graph.

commonNbrs.note: The common neighbours of a tuple of vertices.

biHom.note: The homomorphisms from K_{s,t}: an s-tuple and a t-tuple with every pair adjacent. Checked on K3: 18 for (2,2), agreeing with the closed-4-walk count walk4 as it must since C4 = K_{2,2}, and 24 for (1,3), the star count.

sidorenko_biclique.note: THEOREM 10.3.6 (Sidorenko for complete bipartite graphs) IN FULL: hom(K_{s,t},G) n^(2st-s-t) >= (2m)^(st). The notes demonstrate the case K_{2,2} by entropy and remark that the same proof extends to all K_{s,t}; with the star case in hand the extension needs no entropy at all -- power mean over the n^s tuples, then the star bound on sum_a N(a) = sum_b d(b)^s. Parametrised by s+1 and t+1 so every exponent is a genuine natural number with no truncated subtraction. This SUBSUMES both earlier cases: s = t = 1 is C4 and s = 0 is the star.

cond_indep.note: CONDITIONAL INDEPENDENCE, the step the notes invoke as '[cond indep]' and this library lacked: if the conditional distribution of X given (Y,Z) depends only on Y, then H(X|Y,Z) = H(X|Y). The proof is a regrouping rather than an inequality -- the fibres of (Y,Z) above a fixed Y-value all carry the same conditional distribution, so their weights collapse onto the marginal of Y via sum_wdist_pair_right. Recorded twice in the roadmap as the missing tool for 10.3.5 (all trees) and the notes' own route to 10.3.6; adding it removes that gap from the LIBRARY, though each application still has to verify the hypothesis for its own distribution, which for trees means building the tree-indexed Markov distribution.

hamDist.note: The Hamming distance on the cube, encoded as Finset (Fin n) -- the same subset encoding Chapter 5 uses. Checked: hamDist {0} {1} = 2.

cubeNbhd.note: The t-neighbourhood of a set of points of the cube.

lowBall.note: The Hamming ball about the empty set: points of weight below k.

cube_ball_expand.note: THE t-NEIGHBOURHOOD OF A HAMMING BALL IS A HAMMING BALL, radius grown by exactly t. This is what Theorem 9.4.5's proof uses to evaluate |B_t|, and it is exact rather than approximate. 1 <= k is needed: the ball of radius 0 is empty and expands to nothing. Checked on the 3-cube: the 1-neighbourhood of {empty set} has 4 points, as does the ball of radius 2.

cube_chernoff_ball.note: At least (1 - exp(-2t^2/n)) 2^n points of the cube have weight below n/2 + t. This needed nothing new: Chapter 5's card_filter_sign_sum_le at lambda = 2t/sqrt(n) gives exp(-lambda^2/2) = exp(-2t^2/n) ON THE NOSE, so the constant in Theorem 9.4.5 is exactly the Chernoff constant.

cube_half_ball.note: The half-cube ball has at most 2^(n-1) points, which is what makes Harper applicable to any A with |A| >= 2^(n-1). Complementation is injective and maps the ball into its own complement. Checked: 4 points on the 3-cube (tight) and 5 on the 4-cube.

harper.note: HARPER'S ISOPERIMETRIC INEQUALITY in the Hamming cube (Theorem 9.4.3): among sets of a given size a Hamming ball has the smallest t-neighbourhood. Balls centred at the empty set suffice, since translation by any point is an isometry of the cube. The notes state it WITHOUT PROOF -- it is the hard input of 9.4, by a compression argument -- so it is published as a task rather than assumed silently. STATEMENT COMMITTED.

rapid_expansion_half.note: THEOREM 9.4.5 (rapid expansion from half), CONDITIONAL ON HARPER: if |A| >= 2^(n-1) then |A_t| >= (1 - exp(-2t^2/n)) 2^n. Harper's conclusion for the half-cube ball is an EXPLICIT HYPOTHESIS rather than a use of the sorry'd statement, so this theorem is sorry-free and axiom-clean, and what is missing is visible in the statement. That is the honest way to record a derivation whose one input is a published task.

hamDist_triangle.note: The Hamming distance satisfies the triangle inequality: S \ U is contained in (S \ T) union (T \ U) and symmetrically.

cubeNbhd_compose.note: Expanding twice expands by the sum of the radii, which is what lets Theorem 9.4.6 apply 9.4.5 a second time.

rapid_expansion_eps.note: THEOREM 9.4.6 (rapid expansion from epsilon to 1 - epsilon), CONDITIONAL ON HARPER: with epsilon = exp(-2t^2/n), which is the notes' t = sqrt(n log(1/epsilon)/2), a set of more than epsilon 2^n points expands in 2t steps to more than (1 - epsilon) 2^n. Harper enters as a hypothesis in exactly the form task #46 will prove, so this is sorry-free. ERRATUM-ADJACENT: the hypothesis here is STRICT where the notes write |A| >= epsilon 2^n, and the strictness is needed -- at |A| = epsilon 2^n exactly the counting step gives 2^n <= 2^n and no contradiction. The notes' proof quietly uses a strict Chernoff bound at that point.

homSet.note: The graph homomorphisms from F to G, the object Sidorenko's conjecture is about. Checked: a single edge into K3 has 6 homomorphisms, which is 2m.

sidorenko_tree.note: THEOREM 10.3.5 (Sidorenko for all trees). STATEMENT COMMITTED, published as a task. The cases already proved -- three-edge path, stars, complete bipartite -- were reachable because the homomorphism count factorises outright; a general tree needs the notes' actual argument, a distribution built by picking a root edge and then each further vertex as a uniform neighbour of its parent, with the chain rule along the tree and wcondEntropy_pair_eq_of_condIndep. Stated so that no exponent needs truncated subtraction: multiplying the notes' form by n turns hom n^(e-1) >= (2m)^e into hom n^e >= (2m)^e n, which also reads correctly at e = 0. Checked consistent at e = 1 (a single edge into K3: 6*3 <= 6*3, equality).

hoeffding_lemma.note: HOEFFDING'S LEMMA in finite form, the analytic input of Section 9.1's bounded differences inequality. STATEMENT COMMITTED, published as a task. Mathlib has it for MEASURES (hasSubgaussianMGF_of_mem_Icc_of_integral_eq_zero) via tilted measures and the cumulant generating function; using that here would need a finite-weight-to-Measure bridge, so either route is acceptable. The constant matters: lambda^2 (b-a)^2 / 8 is what makes 9.1.1 come out with the notes' exp(-2 lambda^2 / sum c_i^2), and a cruder MGF bound would be a factor of four worse in the exponent and would NOT prove the theorem as stated. Section 9.1 is the one part of Chapter 9 that lives naturally in the finite framework: the martingale is the sequence of partial averages over the remaining coordinates.

pAvg.note: The average over the uniform product measure on Fin N -> beta, and PMC.avgLast the operation of averaging out the last coordinate -- the Doob martingale's step, made concrete.

bddDiff.note: Bounded differences: changing coordinate i alone moves f by at most c i.

bddDiff_avgLast.note: Averaging out the last coordinate preserves bounded differences WITH THE SAME CONSTANTS, which is what lets the Doob induction recurse.

bounds_last.note: The last-coordinate increment is centred and confined to an interval of length at most c (last N) -- exactly Hoeffding's hypotheses. The interval is exhibited by Finset.inf' and sup' over the coordinate, and the spread is bounded because the extremes differ in that coordinate only.

mgf_bddDiff.note: The sub-Gaussian moment bound E[exp(lambda (f - E f))] <= exp(lambda^2 sum c_i^2 / 8), by induction on the number of coordinates: peel the last one with Fin.snoc, apply Hoeffding to its centred increment, recurse on avgLast f. Hoeffding's lemma enters as the HYPOTHESIS HoeffdingUnif, so this is sorry-free.

mcdiarmid.note: THEOREM 9.1.1 (the bounded differences inequality, McDiarmid): #{x : f x >= E f + t} <= |beta|^N exp(-2t^2 / sum c_i^2). Markov on the moment generating function at the optimal lambda = 4t / sum c_i^2. Hoeffding's lemma is a hypothesis (task #47), so the theorem is sorry-free and axiom-clean, and PMC.hoeffdingUnif_of_hoeffding records the exact instantiation that will discharge it. This is the one part of Chapter 9 that lives naturally in the finite framework: the martingale is the sequence of averages over the remaining coordinates, with no filtration, no conditional expectation operator and no MeasureTheory. Non-vacuity checked by discharging every hypothesis except Hoeffding on a one-coordinate Boolean example.

hoeffding_bridge.note: The bridge from task #47: Hoeffding's lemma for an arbitrary finite weight, instantiated at the uniform weight on one coordinate, is exactly HoeffdingUnif. Stated as an implication so it is itself sorry-free.

mcdiarmid_lower.note: The lower tail of the bounded differences inequality, by applying the upper tail to -f (BddDiff is symmetric under negation). The notes state both tails.

mcdiarmid_one.note: THEOREM 9.1.1 exactly as the notes state it: all constants 1, both tails, bound exp(-2t^2/N). The general-constants form is Theorem 9.1.3, which is PMC.card_filter_ge_le -- the notes give 9.1.1 first and then remark that it holds with per-coordinate constants, so the general one was proved first here and 9.1.1 specialised from it.

missing.note: The number of coupon types a draw sequence misses -- Example 9.1.2's random variable.

bddDiff_missing.note: Changing one draw changes the number of missed types by at most one: the two images differ by at most the replaced coupon on either side, so each missed-set is contained in the other's insert.

pAvg_missing.note: The expected number of missed types is EXACTLY n (1 - 1/n)^n: each type is missed by (n-1)^n of the n^n draws, counted by Fintype.card_piFinset_const, and the double count is a Finset.sum_comm. Checked on Fin 2, where the four draws miss 1,0,0,1 types and the average is 1/2 = 2 (1 - 1/2)^2.

coupon_collector.note: EXAMPLE 9.1.2 (coupon collector), DONE: at most a 2 exp(-2t^2/n) fraction of the n^n draws miss the mean number of missed types by t or more. Theorem 9.1.1 applied with all constants 1, plus the exact mean; the two tails are combined by a union bound. The sample space Fin n -> Fin n is exactly the shape the bounded-differences development uses, so no bridging was needed.

chromNat.note: The chromatic number as a natural number, the least k for which the graph is k-colourable. A Fintype graph is always card-V-colourable, so the minimum exists; using Nat.find rather than Mathlib's ENat-valued chromaticNumber keeps the arithmetic in the reals downstream.

chrom_diff.note: Changing the edges at ONE VERTEX changes the chromatic number by at most one: a proper colouring of the old graph becomes one of the new graph after giving that vertex a fresh colour. This is the graph-theoretic input of Theorem 9.3.1, and the notes give exactly this one-line reason.

graphOf.note: The vertex-exposure encoding: the graph on Fin n where the edge {a,b} with a < b is controlled by coordinate b, the larger endpoint. So coordinate i controls exactly the edges from i downwards, and coordinate 0 controls none. The notes use a product of factors of DIFFERENT sizes (Omega_i = {0,1}^(i-1)); this uses the uniform product Fin n -> (Fin n -> Bool) instead, which is what the bounded-differences development is stated for, at the cost of some redundant coordinates that no lemma has to mention.

graphOf_zero.note: Coordinate 0 controls no edge, so the graph does not depend on it -- which is why its bounded-difference constant is 0 and the window comes out as sqrt(n-1) rather than sqrt(n), exactly as the notes have it. This is where the general-constants form of the inequality (Theorem 9.1.3) earns its keep over the all-ones form (9.1.1).

chrom_concentration.note: THEOREM 9.3.1 (Shamir-Spencer 1987), DONE: P(|chi - E chi| >= lambda sqrt(n-1)) <= 2 exp(-2 lambda^2). A FINITE statement with no o(1) anywhere, and the flagship application of 9.1 -- as the notes put it, concentration around the mean without even knowing where the mean is. Theorem 9.1.3 applied to the vertex-exposure encoding; Hoeffding's lemma (task #47) enters as a hypothesis, so the theorem is sorry-free and axiom-clean.

fHamDist.note: The Hamming distance on the cube written as Fin n -> Bool, the shape Section 9.1's development uses. Checked: two points of the 3-cube differing in two coordinates are at distance 2, and the 1-neighbourhood of a point of the 2-cube has 3 points.

distToSet.note: The distance from a cube point to a nonempty set, as a real -- the random variable the second proof of 9.4.6 concentrates.

bddDiff_distToSet.note: The distance to a set has bounded differences 1: changing one coordinate changes the distance to each point by at most one, and the inf inherits that.

rapid_expansion_harper_free.note: THEOREM 9.4.6 WITHOUT HARPER, the notes' SECOND proof: with epsilon = exp(-2t^2/n), a set of more than epsilon 2^n cube points expands in 2t steps to at least (1-epsilon) 2^n. Apply the bounded differences inequality to f = dist(., A): it vanishes on A, which is more than an epsilon fraction, so the lower tail forces E f < t, and the upper tail then puts all but an epsilon fraction within 2t of A. Compare rapid_expansion_eps, the same statement in the SUBSET encoding, which follows the notes' first proof and therefore carries Harper as a hypothesis -- this version carries none, only Hoeffding via 9.1. Both encodings are kept deliberately: a transfer layer whose only purpose is to restate a proved theorem is not worth its weight.

wHamDist.note: The weighted Hamming distance: the total weight of the coordinates where two points differ. Checked on the 2-cube.

wDistToSet.note: The weighted distance to a set, defined to be 0 on the empty set so that it is total.

wDistToSet_bound.note: For a unit weight vector the weighted distance is at most sqrt(n), by Cauchy-Schwarz over the coordinates where the points differ. This is what makes the supremum defining the convex distance a genuine real number rather than a junk value.

convexDist.note: TALAGRAND'S CONVEX DISTANCE: the supremum of the weighted distance over the unit sphere of nonnegative weights, as an sSup. Nonempty and bounded above, so well defined. Vanishes on A (convexDist_eq_zero_of_mem) and is nonnegative.

hammingLipschitz.note: 1-Lipschitz for the Hamming distance, the hypothesis Theorem 9.5.21 puts on f.

certifiable.note: s-certifiability: membership in a set is always witnessed by at most s coordinates, so any point agreeing there also belongs. This is the combinatorial hypothesis that makes Talagrand's inequality applicable without any geometry.

card_disagree.note: A point far below r must disagree with a certificate on at least t coordinates: otherwise SPLICING the certificate's coordinates in moves f by less than t and lands above r. The splice is the same device Product.lean uses for block independence.

unit_indicator.note: The normalised indicator of a nonempty coordinate set is a nonnegative unit weight vector -- the witness Theorem 9.5.21 feeds to the convex distance.

talagrand_certifiable.note: THEOREM 9.5.21 (Talagrand's inequality for certifiable functions), proved GIVEN Talagrand's inequality as a hypothesis: P(f <= r - t) P(f >= r) <= exp(-t^2/(4s)) for f 1-Lipschitz in Hamming distance with {f >= r} s-certifiable. This is the COMBINATORIAL half of 9.5 and needed no convex geometry -- the normalised indicator of a certificate is already a unit weight vector witnessing d_T(y,A) >= t/sqrt(s), and the rest is counting. It is also the form the section's applications use (longest increasing subsequence, Euclidean TSP). Sorry-free: Talagrand enters as the hypothesis in exactly the form task #49 proves.

lisLength.note: The length of the longest increasing subsequence, as the sup of the sizes of increasing index sets. Checked on the identity sequence of Fin 3, where it is 3.

lis_lipschitz.note: lisLength is 1-Lipschitz for the Hamming distance. The general bound comes from deleting the disagreeing indices from a witness: what is left is increasing for the other point, so the length drops by at most the number of disagreements.

lis_certifiable.note: {lis >= k} is k-CERTIFIABLE: k indices of a witnessing subsequence certify it, since any point agreeing there has the same subsequence increasing. This is why s-certifiability is the right hypothesis in 9.5.21 -- it is exactly what 'a witness of size s' means.

lis_concentration.note: COROLLARY 9.5.23's CONTENT, given Talagrand: #{x : lis x <= k - t} * #{x : lis x >= k} <= |beta|^(2n) exp(-t^2/(4k)). The notes wrap this in an asymptotic statement about the median (P(|X - MX| <= C n^(1/4)) >= 1 - eps); the inequality itself is finite and is what 9.5.21 delivers directly, so it is what gets stated here.

exists_le_wmean.note: SOME POINT IS AT MOST THE AVERAGE, in weighted form -- the probabilistic method's core move, now centralised rather than re-derived per application (Chapters 1, 2 and 3 each did it by hand with Finset.exists_le_of_sum_le). PMC.exists_wmean_le is the other half.

lll_quarter.note: COROLLARY 6.1.10: if every bad event has probability below 1/2 and the probabilities in each neighbourhood sum to at most 1/4, then with positive probability none occurs. The asymmetric local lemma at x_i = 2 P(A_i), where the required bound becomes 1/2 <= prod (1 - 2 P(A_j)) and the WEIERSTRASS PRODUCT INEQUALITY 1 - sum y <= prod (1 - y) supplies it. That inequality is not in Mathlib and is proved here as a two-line induction.

entropy_indep.note: LEMMA 10.1.5 (independence): H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y) for independent X and Y. By the chain rule it suffices that conditioning on X does nothing, which independence gives on every fibre of positive weight; the zero-weight fibres contribute nothing to either side.

jPairs.note: The overlapping ordered pairs with the second index smaller -- the index set of Zhao's Delta/2, as a single Finset of pairs rather than a nested sum. Making it one sum is what lets the second-moment computation go through cleanly.

jHalfDelta.note: Delta/2 restricted to a subfamily, plus jMu for mu. jHalfDelta_eq identifies it with the nested double sum janson_upper uses.

janson_sub.note: Janson I for a SUBFAMILY. Nothing new was needed: janson_prod_le was already stated for an arbitrary T, so the proof of janson_upper applies verbatim -- which is what made the sampling argument available.

bweight_second_moment.note: The second moment of the random subfamily: E[Delta_T] = q^2 Delta. Swap the sum over subfamilies with the sum over pairs, and sum_bweight_mem_pair gives q^(#{i,j}) = q^2 for each pair, distinct because the second index is strictly smaller.

janson_II.note: THEOREM 8.1.8 (Janson inequality II), DONE: if mu <= Delta then P(X = 0) <= exp(-mu^2/(2 Delta)). Janson I is strong only when Delta = o(mu); this covers the other regime. The notes' SAMPLING proof: apply Janson I to a random subfamily keeping each index with probability q = mu/Delta, whose moments are q mu and q^2 Delta, and take a subfamily at least as good as the average (exists_le_wmean). mu <= Delta is exactly what makes q <= 1. Both ingredients were already in the library -- janson_prod_le's arbitrary subfamily and bweight's moments -- so what this needed was the pair-sum bookkeeping connecting them. Found by the coverage audit; sorry-free and independent of task #42.

two_coloring_nonuniform.note: THEOREM 6.2.6 (finite case): a hypergraph whose edges all have size AT LEAST k, each meeting at most d others, is 2-colourable once e (d+1) 2^(1-k) <= 1. The generalisation of 6.2.1 from k-uniform to non-uniform cost nothing: the monochromatic probability of an edge of size m is 2^(1-m) <= 2^(1-k), and the symmetric local lemma only ever wanted an UPPER bound on the probabilities. Theorem 6.2.1 is now the uniform corollary. The notes also state 6.2.6 for infinite vertex sets, which needs their compactness Lemma 6.2.7 and is not claimed here.

two_coloring_regular.note: COROLLARY 6.2.2: for k >= 9, every k-uniform k-regular hypergraph is 2-colourable. The degree count is the content -- an edge has k vertices, each in k edges, one of which is the edge itself, so it meets at most k(k-1) others (a biUnion bound over the edge's vertices). The numeric side condition 2e(k^2-k+1) <= 2^k is an induction from k = 9, where 2e*73 = 396.9 <= 512; the step needs only k^2 - 3k + 1 >= 0, true from k = 3, so 9 is forced by the BASE case rather than the induction.

monotone_family.note: A monotone (upward-closed) family of subsets, with the two endpoint lemmas: upward-closure makes 'non-trivial' equivalent to the empty set not being a member and the whole set being one.

threshold_strictmono.note: THEOREM 4.3.5 (monotonicity of the satisfying probability). STATEMENT COMMITTED, published as a task. Section 4.3's threshold results are asymptotic and stay deferred, but 4.3.5 is NOT -- it is a finite statement about a polynomial in p, and it is the fact every later threshold argument silently uses. The route: with independent coordinate probabilities the weight of F is LINEAR in each p_j, and upward-closure gives P(F | j in S) >= P(F | j not in S) by the injection S -> S union {j}, so P is nondecreasing in every coordinate; strictness needs one pivotal coordinate, which non-triviality supplies from a minimal member of F.
