indepSets.note: The independent sets of a graph, and the two products: twoAdj (two disjoint copies) and coverAdj (the bipartite double cover G x K_2). Both are given as RELATIONS on V x Bool rather than SimpleGraph structures -- independence only needs the relation, so there are no symm or loopless obligations. Checked: i(K2) = 3 with cover count 9, i(K3) = 4 with cover count 18.

card_indepTwo.note: i(2G) = i(G)^2: an independent set of two disjoint copies is exactly a pair of independent sets, one per copy.

swapSet.note: Swapping the two copies of every vertex of A. An INVOLUTION (swapSet_swapSet), which is what makes the injection recoverable.

crossing_slice.note: THE BAD EDGES ARE BIPARTITE, witnessed by the copy-0 slice: a bad edge has its first endpoint there and, since S is independent in 2G, its second endpoint not. This is what guarantees a crossing set exists at all.

swap_repairs.note: SWAPPING REPAIRS EVERY BAD EDGE: the swapped set is independent in the cover. Four cases on which endpoints lie in A -- two give two vertices of S in the SAME copy, contradicting independence in 2G, and the other two give a bad edge with both endpoints on the same side of A, contradicting the crossing property.

swap_recovery.note: THE IMAGE REMEMBERS THE BAD EDGES: after swapping along a crossing set, the same-copy adjacent pairs of the image are exactly the bad edges of the original, in either orientation. With crossing_iff_crossingT this makes the whole crossing FAMILY -- and hence the canonical choice made from it -- recoverable from the image, which is the crux of injectivity.

swapping_lemma.note: LEMMA 10.4.13 (the bipartite swapping trick), DONE and UNCONDITIONAL: i(G)^2 <= i(G x K_2). This is what reduces Kahn-Zhao (10.4.12) from all d-regular graphs to the bipartite ones, and unlike the rest of 10.4 it is not an entropy argument at all -- the notes give an explicit injection and this formalises it. The canonical choice of crossing set is made by PICKMIN, a function of the crossing FAMILY alone (least index under a fixed indexing of the subsets), which is precisely what injectivity needs. Checked: equality at K2 (9 = 3^2, the cover being two disjoint edges) and strict at K3 (16 <= 18, the cover being a 6-cycle).

shearer_subset.note: Shearer's lemma for a SUB-tuple: k*H(X_S) <= sum_j H(X_{A_j}) when the A_j all lie in S and every coordinate OF S is covered k times. The coordinates outside S need no cover, which required weakening shearer_of_submodular's hypothesis to allow null coordinates (shearer_of_submodular_null). Kahn-Zhao needs exactly this: it covers one side A of the bipartition by the neighbourhoods N(b), and the vertices of B lie in none of them.

gibbs_variational.note: THE GIBBS VARIATIONAL PRINCIPLE: H(Z) + E[a(Z)] <= log sum_{t in T} exp (a t) for Z supported in T, with equality at the Gibbs measure. The a = 0 case is the existing 'entropy at most log support' bound. This is where Kahn-Zhao's constant 2^(d+1)-1 = i(K_{d,d}) comes from, with a reason attached rather than by exhibiting the extremal graph.

cond_copies.note: d+1 CONDITIONALLY INDEPENDENT COPIES, the device the notes describe in words ('let X' be a conditionally independent copy of X given Y'). sum_condProd is the normalisation, condProd_marginal_zero says a coordinate carries the original law. Used by the notes' own 10.3 proofs; Kahn-Zhao as formalized here does NOT need it, since the Gibbs variational principle replaces the copies.

kahn_zhao_bipartite.note: KAHN's BIPARTITE CASE of Theorem 10.4.12: i(G)^d <= (2^(d+1)-1)^#B for a d-regular graph with bipartition V = A + B. Shearer on the A side (covering multiplicity = regularity), chain rule with block subadditivity on the B side, and one per-vertex maximisation for each b in B. The per-vertex step departs from the notes: instead of d conditionally independent copies it uses that X_b is determined unless X_{N(b)} is all-false, plus the Gibbs variational principle.

kahn_zhao.note: THEOREM 10.4.12 (Kahn, Zhao), DONE: i(G)^(2d) <= (2^(d+1)-1)^n for every n-vertex d-regular graph. Stated over the naturals -- the notes' i(G) <= i(K_{d,d})^{n/(2d)} with the root cleared, equivalent by monotonicity of log. Zhao's reduction: the double cover is bipartite and d-regular, Kahn's case applies to it, and the swapping trick transfers the bound back. Checked by brute force over every regular graph on at most 6 vertices: no violations, and the equality cases are exactly the disjoint unions of K_{d,d}.

galvin_tetali.note: THEOREM 10.4.14 (Galvin-Tetali 2004), DONE: hom(G,H)^d <= hom(K_{d,d},H)^#B for d-regular bipartite G and any target H with loops allowed. The notes state it and say only that Kahn's proof 'extends'; it does, and the extension was cheap because the global argument was first factored out as mul_tupleEntropy_univ_le. The per-vertex bound is the Gibbs variational principle at the energy d*log #commonNbhd, whose partition function IS hom(K_{d,d},H) by card_kddHom -- so the extremal graph arrives as the partition function rather than as an example. Degenerate tuples must be excluded from that sum: log 0 = 0 makes exp(d log 0) = 1 where #commonNbhd^d = 0. Checked by brute force over all targets on <= 3 vertices, and in Lean: at indepTarget it reproduces card_indepR_pow_le_of_bipartite.

ham_cycles.note: LEMMA 10.2.7 plus THEOREM 10.2.4's lower bound, DONE: an (m+1)-vertex tournament with P Hamilton paths extends by a vertex to one with at least P/4 Hamilton cycles, so some (m+2)-vertex tournament has (m+1)! <= 4*#cycles*2^m. 2 <= n is NECESSARY: for a one-vertex path the two closing constraints fall on the same edge, and a 2-vertex tournament has a Hamilton path but no Hamilton cycle. Cycles are counted as the orderings starting at the NEW vertex, which is an honest count (each directed cycle meets it once) and avoids dividing by n. The averaging is a double count of orientation/path pairs, exact in the checked cases: sum over orientations of #cycles is 6 = 3*2^3/4 for the 3-cycle and 2 = 1*2^3/4 for the transitive tournament.

latin_transversal.note: THEOREM 6.5.11 (Erdos-Spencer 1991), the original application of the lopsided local lemma: an n x n array whose every entry appears at most m times with 4em <= n has a Latin transversal. The negative-dependence input (Theorem 6.5.5, waiting on task #44) is an EXPLICIT HYPOTHESIS in the shape lovasz_local_lemma_symmetric_lopsided consumes, so the theorem is sorry-free and independent of exists_perm_extend's sorry. Proved here: the degree count #N(p) <= 4n(m-1) by covering the neighbourhood with a biUnion over p's four lines, and the arithmetic e(4n(m-1)+2) <= n(n-1). Each unordered bad pair must be ONE index -- ordered pairs double the degree and the constant does not survive that. Spot-checked on the cyclic Latin square of order 3: 9 bad pairs, max degree 9, bound 24.

dubroff_fox_xu.note: THEOREM 4.6.6 (Dubroff-Fox-Xu 2021): k integers bounded by n with distinct subset sums force C(k,floor(k/2)) <= n. The reduction is proved in full -- card_lowHalf (the below-half subsets are exactly half the cube, distinctness ruling out the tie with the complement) and card_boundary_lowHalf_le (a boundary point is an insertion, never an erasure, so its sum lies in an interval of n integers on which distinctness makes the sum injective). Harper is an explicit hypothesis in BOUNDARY form, which the ball form of task #46 does not reach for even k. STATEMENT BUG CAUGHT BY BRUTE FORCE: the hypothesis was first written with 2^(k-1) <= #A, which is false at A = univ and would have made the theorem vacuous; the equality form is true and tight for k <= 4.

triangle_threshold.note: PROP 4.1.2 and THEOREM 4.1.11, the triangle threshold, in the notes' own asymptotic phrasing: np -> 0 gives triangle-free with probability 1-o(1), np -> infinity gives a triangle with probability 1-o(1). The limits sit ON TOP OF explicit bounds rather than replacing them, so the convention on asymptotics is unchanged and nothing about the finite framework had to move. The real work was the SHARPER VARIANCE wvar_card_triangles_le': Var <= C(n,3)(p^3 + 3n p^5). The earlier bound (every overlapping pair <= p^3) gives P(triangle-free) <~ 1/(n^2 p^3), which diverges at p = n^(-9/10) and so cannot prove 4.1.11 at all; separating the two overlap classes (t'=t contributes p^3 once, #(t inter t')=2 contributes p^5 at most 3n times) fixes it.

janson_triangle.note: COROLLARY 8.1.7, DONE: P(G(n,c/n) triangle-free) -> e^{-c^3/6}. Needed Janson specialized to triangles (probTriangleFree_le_exp: mu = C(n,3)p^3, Delta <= 3n C(n,3) p^5, using that two distinct triples share an edge iff they share two vertices and then span 5 edges) plus the Harris lower bound already proved. NO LOGARITHMS: both bracketing inequalities for 1-u are Real.add_one_le_exp, the second applied at u/(1-u) and multiplied by exp(-u/(1-u)). The index type is Fin (C(n,3)) with an explicit enumeration because janson's upper half needs a linear order on the index and transporting one onto Finset would bring its own DecidableEq. Checked by simulation at c=1,2 and n=10,20,40: the simulated probability sits between the brackets and both close on the limit.

clique_threshold.note: THEOREM 4.2.5 (first half) and THEOREM 4.4.2(a): the probability of containing a k-clique vanishes as soon as the expected number C(n,k)p^C(k,2) does. Markov plus a squeeze; the two named instances are p << n^(-2/3) giving no K4 whp and f(n,k) -> 0 giving omega(G(n,1/2)) < k whp. The second-moment halves are not proved -- they need Delta* for k-cliques, the k-vertex analogue of wvar_card_triangles_le', and 4.1 showed a crude version of that does not reach the threshold.

cheap_sampling.note: PROPOSITION 2.4.2: a tetrahedron-free 3-graph on n >= 4 vertices has 4#H <= 3C(n,3). The same double count as 2.4.4 with four vertices instead of five, where the base case IS the hypothesis. The pair 2.4.2/2.4.4 shows what sampling one more vertex buys (3/4 -> 7/10) and costs (a base case, which is also where the notes' n >= 4 slips to n >= 5).

median_talagrand.note: COROLLARY 9.5.22 plus the median it needs. exists_isMedian builds a median for any real-valued function on a nonempty finite type by counting, not compactness: take the least attained value with half the points below it, and minimality forces half at or above. Then Talagrand's product bound at r = M gives P(f <= M - t) <= 2 exp(-t^2/(4s)), since a median makes the second factor at least 1/2. Kept in a separate file because Talagrand.lean holds task #49's target and is left byte-for-byte as published.

measure_bridge.note: THE MEASURE BRIDGE: a finite weight packaged as a PMF, with wmean identified with the Bochner integral against its measure. Costs two instances (the discrete sigma-algebra on a finite type and its MeasurableSingletonClass) and nothing else. With it Mathlib's probability library applies to this development: it closed task #47 (Hoeffding's lemma) from hasSubgaussianMGF_of_mem_Icc_of_integral_eq_zero, which in turn made 9.1.1, 9.1.3, 9.1.2, 9.3.1 and 9.4.6 unconditional and unblocked Corollary 5.0.6. Azuma-Hoeffding and the martingale library are now reachable the same way.

hoeffding_bernoulli.note: COROLLARY 5.0.6, both tails: P(X >= mu + t) <= exp(-2t^2/n) and the notes' P(X >= mu + lambda sqrt n) <= e^{-lambda^2/2}. Engine: Hoeffding's lemma at a SINGLE Bernoulli (bernoulli_mgf_le, from wmean_exp_le_of_mem_Icc on the two-point space), multiplied over coordinates against the exact MGF already proved for 5.0.7, then Markov at lambda = 4t/n. The lower tail is complementation, not a second argument: pweight (1-p) of the complement equals pweight p.
